# The Self and Self-Realization

The self is not only the centre but also the whole circumference which embraces both conscious and unconscious; it is the centre of this totality, just as the ego is the centre of the conscious mind. The self is the total, timeless man who stands for the mutual integration of conscious and unconscious. The realization of the self is the goal of the individuation process.

The symbols of the self arise in the depths of the body and they express its materiality every bit as much as the structure of the perceiving consciousness. The symbol of the self is the mandala, the magic circle, which appears spontaneously in dreams and in the art of all cultures. It expresses the totality of the psyche in all its aspects, including the relationship between man and the whole of nature.

The transcendent function arises from the union of conscious and unconscious contents. It is not something that the ego can produce at will; it comes about naturally as a result of the confrontation between the conscious standpoint and the unconscious compensation. When thesis and antithesis are held together in the psyche, the transcendent function bridges the gap and produces a new synthesis — a transformation of personality that neither the conscious position nor the unconscious alone could have achieved.

Self-realization is not the same as ego-inflation. The self is an empirical concept designating the whole range of psychic phenomena in man. It expresses the unity and wholeness of the total personality. As an empirical concept, the self designates the whole range of psychic phenomena in man. To the extent that the individual remains unconscious of the self, it appears projected onto something else — a leader, a cause, an institution, or a divine figure.
